intro.html: Some speakers never quite tell a lie, yet you leave the conversation knowing less than when you started. They hint instead of saying, dodge instead of answering, and dress up weak reasons in fancy words. This topic names their moves.
When you read an argument, these words help you say exactly what is wrong with it: not just “I don’t trust him,” but “his answer was evasive, and his reasoning was sophistry.”

words.def: smooth and quick with words but shallow or insincere
words.ex: The salesman had a {glib} answer for every question but never once looked us in the eye.
words.ctx: Her apology sounded {glib}: she rattled it off in two seconds, flashed a smile and went right back to her game.

mn.text: Victor’s words glide off his lips like skates on ice: fast, smooth and with nothing underneath. His talk is {glib}.

labels.text: GL-IB: words GLIDE off the LIPS

scene.alt: A smooth-talking man winks into a microphone on stage while a doubtful old man folds his arms.

words.def: to hint at something unpleasant without saying it outright
words.ex: Are you trying to {insinuate} that I ate the last cookie?
words.ctx: Rex never said outright that Lila had copied her essay; instead he {insinuated} it, raising his eyebrows and asking how she had finished so fast.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin insinuare, “to wind one’s way in”: in- (in) + sinuare (to curve), from sinus (a curve).

mn.text: Pip looks at the empty cookie jar, then slowly at Kai, and says, “Hmm, someone ate them...” He does not accuse Kai directly; he {insinuates} it.

scene.alt: A boy eyes an empty cookie plate and then his nervous friend, hinting that the friend ate the cookies.

words.def: a sly, indirect hint, usually an unkind one about someone
words.ex: The gossip column was full of {innuendo} but had not a single fact.
words.ctx: The rival bakery never accused Nell outright; it spread {innuendo} instead, wondering aloud why her kitchen was always closed on Mondays.
words.etym: From Latin innuendo, “by nodding at,” from innuere (to nod to, to hint).
words.note: The plural is innuendos or innuendoes.

mn.cue: a NOD and a WINK, not a word
mn.text: At the bake sale, Greta winks and murmurs, “Some people’s homemade pies come from a box, I hear...” That sly, unkind hint is {innuendo}.

labels.text: IN-NU-ENDO: a NOD and a WINK

scene.alt: At a bake sale, a woman winks and whispers an unkind hint about the baker, who looks annoyed.

words.def: avoiding a direct answer or a clear statement
words.ex: When asked where the cake had gone, the twins gave {evasive} answers about the weather.
words.ctx: Usually Dev answered questions in detail, but about his report card he was strangely {evasive}, changing the subject every time his mother brought it up.
words.etym: From evade, from Latin evadere, “to go out, to escape”: e- (out) + vadere (to go).

mn.cue: EVADE the question like a dodgeball
mn.text: Granny Mae asks who broke the lamp, and Pip ducks the question like a dodgeball: “Nice weather, huh?” His answer is {evasive}.

scene.alt: A grandmother asks who broke the lamp, and a boy dodges sideways, talking about the weather.

words.def: to use vague or double-meaning words to avoid taking a clear position
words.ex: Asked if he liked the new haircut, Dad {equivocated}: “Well, it’s certainly... different.”
words.ctx: Instead of saying yes or no, the coach began to {equivocate}, talking about “options” and “seeing how things go” until the players gave up asking.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Late Latin aequivocus, “having the same sound, meaning two things”: aequi- (equal) + vox (voice).

mn.cue: EQUAL VOICES: yes AND no at once
mn.text: Asked if he likes Aunt Tia’s purple soup, Sami says, “Well, it’s... very purple!” His answer could mean yes or no; he {equivocates}.

scene.alt: An aunt offers a bowl of purple soup, and a boy shrugs, giving an answer that is neither yes nor no.

words.def: to dodge the truth, often by speaking in a misleading way
words.ex: When the teacher asked about the missing homework, Jonah began to {prevaricate}, spinning a long tale about a windstorm.
words.ctx: The witness did not tell an outright lie, but she {prevaricated}, giving answers so slippery that the jury could not tell what she had really seen.
words.etym: From Latin praevaricari, “to walk crookedly, to straddle,” and so to play false.

mn.text: Caught beside the broken vase, the cat varies its story every minute: first the wind did it, then the dog. That cat loves to {prevaricate}.

scene.alt: A cat beside a broken vase blames the dog, who looks shocked.

words.def: to hide one’s true feelings or aims behind a false show
words.ex: Though she was crushed by the news, Maya {dissembled} and smiled through the whole party.
words.ctx: The spy had to {dissemble} for years, chatting cheerfully with the guards while secretly mapping every hallway of the fortress.
words.etym: From Latin dissimulare, “to hide, to disguise”: dis- (not) + simulare (to make like, to pretend).
words.note: Do not confuse dissemble (hide your feelings) with disassemble (take apart).

mn.cue: a mask that does NOT RESEMBLE you
mn.text: Maya is sad inside, but she holds up a smiling mask that does not resemble her real face at all; to hide your feelings that way is to {dissemble}.

scene.alt: A sad girl on a stage holds up a smiling mask to hide her true feelings.

words.def: to make something confusing or unclear on purpose
words.ex: The instructions were so full of jargon that they seemed meant to {obfuscate} rather than explain.
words.ctx: Rather than admit the mistake, the company tried to {obfuscate} it, burying one honest sentence inside forty pages of technical language.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin obfuscare, “to darken”: ob- (over) + fuscus (dark).

mn.cue: OB-FUSC: make it DARK and murky
mn.text: To slip away, the octopus squirts a cloud of dark ink until no one can see a thing; making things murky on purpose is to {obfuscate}.

scene.alt: An octopus squirts a dark cloud of ink while a confused fish cannot see through it.

words.def: clever-sounding reasoning that is false or misleading
words.ex: His argument that homework is bad because it wastes pencils was pure {sophistry}.
words.ctx: The lawyer’s case sounded brilliant at first, but it was {sophistry}: each step seemed logical, yet together they proved something everyone knew was false.
words.etym: From sophist, from Greek sophistes, “an expert, a wise man”; some teachers called sophists in ancient Greece became known for tricky arguments.

mn.text: Sami proves at the board that cats have four legs, his dog has four legs, so his dog must be a cat; it sounds clever, but it is {sophistry}.

scene.alt: A proud boy in a graduation cap “proves” on the board that his dog is a cat, while the dog looks puzzled.

words.def: to argue or complain about small, unimportant points
words.ex: Let’s not {quibble} over a nickel; just split the bill.
words.ctx: Instead of fixing the big flaws in the plan, the committee spent an hour {quibbling} over whether the posters should be blue or teal.

mn.text: Pip and Lila argue for an hour over who gets the last tiny nibble of cookie; to argue over something that small is to {quibble}.

scene.alt: Two children point and argue across a table over a single tiny crumb of cookie.

head: move
words
what the speaker does
rows: suggests something unkind without saying it
avoids a straight answer; prevaricate comes closest to lying
hides true feelings; makes things murky
smooth but shallow; false reasoning; fusses over trifles

after.html: Insinuate is the verb; innuendo is the noun for the hint itself. And dissemble (hide your feelings) is not disassemble (take apart).

items.q: Though furious, the queen smiled sweetly at her guests. She chose to…
items.why: She hid her true feelings behind a false show: she dissembled. To disassemble is to take something apart.

items.q: Which of these words comes closest to telling an outright lie?
items.why: To prevaricate is to dodge the truth, and it often shades into lying. To equivocate is to stay vague; to quibble is to argue over small points; to insinuate is to hint.
fuscus means dark: to obfuscate is to darken, to make murky and unclear.

items.q: Which word is a noun naming a sly, unkind hint?
items.why: Innuendo is the hint itself. Insinuate is the verb for making one.
